speaker: David Vélez
title: How He Built the World’s Largest Digital Bank with 140 Million Customers | David Vélez
question: When evaluating a digital bank's business model, which financial metrics actually prove a durable competitive moat?
guest: Customer growth, Net Promoter Score, and customer acquisition cost show whether you hit an underserved market with a product nobody else offered. But the next question is whether that growth is sustainable, because you can always buy growth by spending heavily on marketing. So you look at LTV to CAC and ultimately return on equity, which captures the true advantage of the business model. Compared with big incumbent banks in our markets, we charge zero fees—so we generate less revenue per customer—yet we still achieve a return on equity two to three times higher than theirs. That proves you found a structural cost advantage through technology, delivering better quality at a much lower cost, which is a real moat in a commoditized industry like banking. Looking at the US, some incumbent banks actually earn higher ROE than emerging-market banks despite carrying huge physical branch costs—and in the classic 'your margin is my opportunity' sense, that signals significant room to undercut.

points.core: Customer growth alone is inconclusive because banks can buy users through marketing.
points.note: Accept: rapid user growth or high NPS must be paired with CAC, LTV/CAC, or unit-economics discipline because growth can be subsidized by ad spend. Do not credit: listing growth metrics without noting they can be bought unsustainably.

points.core: Outperforming incumbents on ROE despite zero fees proves a structural cost moat.
points.note: Accept: generating higher return on equity (e.g., 2-3x incumbents) with lower fee revenue mathematically demonstrates a superior technology-driven cost structure. Do not credit: saying 'high ROE is good' without connecting it to lower fees/revenue or cost-structure advantage.

points.core: High incumbent bank ROE despite branch overhead signals fat margins ripe for undercutting.
points.note: Accept: when legacy banks earn strong returns even while funding expensive branches and staff, low-cost digital entrants have wide margin headroom to compete on price/yield. Do not credit: generic claims that incumbents are inefficient without tying high incumbent ROE to undercutting opportunity.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
No single metric proves a moat; what matters is a cluster of metrics that hold up together over a full credit and rate cycle.

The strongest evidence is funding advantage: a low cost of deposits relative to peers, with a high share of primary-account, non-interest-bearing balances and a low deposit beta when rates rise. This shows customers stay for reasons other than rate, which is the hardest thing for competitors to copy.

Second is structural cost efficiency: a cost-to-income ratio sustainably below about 35–40% and a falling cost-to-serve per customer as scale grows.

Third is unit economics: customer acquisition cost that stays low (ideally driven by organic or referral growth) against rising revenue per active customer, with strong cohort retention and growing cross-sell.

Fourth is credit quality: risk-adjusted net interest margin and stable cost of risk through a downturn, proving that underwriting, not loose lending, drives growth.

The summary test is return on equity sustainably above cost of capital while still growing. Be sceptical of headline customer counts, growth fuelled by promotional rates, and profitability flattered by a benign credit environment.

points.why: The response explains that promotional incentives can buy customer growth and tests that growth against persistently low acquisition costs.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
A digital bank proves a durable moat not through raw user growth, which is easily bought, but through financial metrics demonstrating customer primacy, structural cost advantages, and underwriting edge. Most critical are a persistently low cost of funding and low deposit beta, driven by high primary-account direct deposits rather than promotional yields, which prove real switching costs. On the expense side, a structurally low monthly cost to serve and an efficiency ratio well below traditional banks’ 50%–60% benchmark confirm genuine technology-driven operating leverage.

Equally telling is cohort-level average revenue per active customer (ARPU) that steadily expands alongside low, mostly organic customer acquisition costs (CAC), showing the bank can cross-sell credit and wealth products without constantly re-buying engagement. Meanwhile, a resilient risk-adjusted net interest margin—interest spreads net of credit losses across a full credit cycle—distinguishes proprietary data underwriting from reckless loan growth. Ultimately, a true moat is proven when these advantages compound into sustained, above-peer return on tangible common equity (ROTCE) without relying on excess leverage or regulatory interchange arbitrage.

points.why: The response explicitly says user growth can be bought and uses low, mostly organic CAC to assess whether acquisition is sustainable.
quotes: raw user growth, which is easily bought
low, mostly organic customer acquisition costs (CAC)

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
No single metric proves a moat. Durability shows up when several unit-economics measures stay strong over time, across customer cohorts and through a credit cycle.

The strongest evidence is a structural cost advantage. That means a low and falling cost to serve each active customer compared with what each customer brings in, and an efficiency ratio that keeps improving as the bank grows. Nubank is the usual example: it serves customers for about a dollar a month and earns several times that from each one.

Next, look at cheap customer acquisition. A high share of organic or referral sign-ups and a short payback period on acquisition spending suggest real brand or network pull rather than paid growth.

Third, check whether the bank has become customers' main bank. Signs include a high share of customers depositing their salary, high monthly activity per customer, a low cost of funds with a low deposit beta (how much of a rate rise it passes on to depositors), and revenue per customer from older cohorts that keeps rising through cross-selling.

Finally, require credit losses that stay disciplined compared with peers through a downturn, and a return on equity that stays above the cost of capital. Fast growth funded by marketing spending or teaser deposit rates does not show a moat.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: A digital bank’s moat is best proven by metrics that separate genuine primary-bank relationships and structural cost advantages from rate-chasing growth. First, watch its cost of funds and deposit beta relative to benchmark rates: a persistently low, stable funding cost—backed by high shares of non-interest-bearing or payroll-linked deposits—proves sticky switching costs rather than hot money attracted by teaser yields. Second, examine risk-adjusted net interest margin and net charge-off rates through a credit cycle to confirm that lending spreads reflect superior underwriting rather than hidden credit risk. Third, a sustainably low efficiency ratio and declining cost to serve per active customer validate true digital operating leverage over branch-heavy incumbents. Finally, pair cohort-level revenue expansion and short customer acquisition cost payback periods with return on tangible common equity (ROTCE). When a digital bank consistently earns ROTCE well above its cost of equity without relying on promotional rates or interchange subsidies, its competitive advantage is durable.

points.why: The response discusses deposits attracted by teaser yields and recommends tracking CAC payback, but it never explains how acquisition spending can inflate customer growth.
The response benchmarks ROTCE against the cost of equity and never shows that the digital bank earns higher returns than incumbents despite charging lower or zero fees.
The response mentions branch-heavy incumbents but never links strong incumbent ROE despite branch overhead to a digital entrant’s ability to undercut them.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A digital bank’s strongest evidence of a durable moat is a sustained return on tangible common equity above its cost of equity and ahead of comparable banks, at similar leverage and risk, through rate and credit cycles. The underlying metrics should show where that excess return comes from.

For a funding moat, look for low all-in deposit costs, a low deposit beta (how much deposit rates rise when market rates rise), and strong retention of customers who use the bank as their primary account. For a distribution moat, look for short customer acquisition payback and rising contribution profit across mature customer cohorts after servicing, rewards, fraud, and credit losses. For a lending moat, look for higher risk-adjusted returns than peers on comparable loans, with losses tracked by origination vintage as loans mature.

The test is whether those advantages persist as the bank scales and competitors respond. Customer growth, headline net interest margin, and a low cost-to-income ratio are useful context.

points.why: The response mentions customer growth and acquisition payback without explaining that marketing spend can buy unsustainable growth.
The response cites peer-beating returns without linking them to lower fee revenue and a technology-driven cost advantage.
The response does not connect high incumbent ROE despite branch overhead to a digital entrant’s ability to undercut incumbents.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
No single metric proves a moat. The strongest evidence is a digital bank consistently earning a return on tangible equity above its cost of equity and above comparable banks’ returns on similar leverage, including when rates change and credit losses rise.

Look for the source of that advantage. A funding moat shows up when customers keep their deposits even as the bank raises deposit rates less than peers. A cost advantage shows up in lower operating costs per active customer at comparable service levels. A distribution advantage shows up when successive customer cohorts stay active and repay their acquisition costs quickly through contribution profit after funding costs, servicing, incentives, and credit losses.

For a lender, compare margins after credit losses on loans of similar age and borrower risk. Fast loan growth can flatter returns before losses surface. Customer growth, app downloads, and a high net interest margin alone tell you little about whether competitors can replicate the economics.

The response discusses superior returns and lower operating costs separately without linking higher returns despite lower fee revenue to a structural cost advantage.
The response does not connect strong incumbent returns despite branch overhead to a digital entrant’s ability to undercut incumbents on price or yield.
